sources.title: Ryuichi Sakamoto (Q345494) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-24): English label 'Ryuichi Sakamoto', description 'Japanese composer, musician, social activist, and former student activist (1952-2023)', Korean label, born 17 January 1952, died 28 March 2023, citizenship Japan. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Rolling Stone Australia, obituary of Ryuichi Sakamoto (2023), read in full via a text fetch: co-founded Yellow Magic Orchestra in 1978 with Yukihiro Takahashi and Haruomi Hosono, using synthesizers, sequencers and drum machines; solo records Thousand Knives (1978) and B-2 Unit (1980, with the electro single 'Riot in Lagos', said to have influenced Afrika Bambaataa and Mantronix); Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence (1983) as his first film score and acting debut (the score later won a BAFTA); The Last Emperor (1987), scored with David Byrne and Cong Su, which won the Academy Award for Best Original Score and a Grammy; later Bertolucci films The Sheltering Sky and Little Buddha, Brian De Palma's Snake Eyes and Femme Fatale, The Revenant (2015, with Alva Noto and Bryce Dessner), async (2017), his label Commmons, and the album 12; Sakamoto saying he never set out to be a professional musician and had hoped to write a novel or make films. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (with the Google Arts & Culture YMO story and the Academy record). Music-press obituary, admiring; the passages on illness and death were not used.

Eiichi Yoshimura, 'How one band shaped the sounds of Japan and beyond', Google Arts & Culture (Yellow Magic Orchestra story; photographs Kenji Miura and Kazuhiro Kitaoka), read in full: the 1978 founding by Haruomi Hosono, Ryuichi Sakamoto and Yukihiro Takahashi, the aim of 'stateless, exotic' sound from disco beats, computers and synthesizers; Sakamoto studied composition at the Tokyo University of the Arts; the 1978 debut (US release 1979), Solid State Survivor (1979, with 'Rydeen' and 'Behind the Mask'), the 1980 world tours, BGM (1981, Roland TR-808 drum machine) and Technodelic (1981, early extensive sampling with a hand-built sampler), the split in 1983 and later regroupings; sampling of 'Computer Game' by later artists. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (with Rolling Stone Australia). Cultural-institution overview of the group, not of Sakamoto alone; admiring.

Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, 60th Academy Awards ceremony page (oscars.org, held 11 April 1988 for films of 1987), checked for the record: The Last Emperor is listed as winner of Music (Original Score), credited to Ryuichi Sakamoto, David Byrne and Cong Su. Award record only; no behavioural claim rests on it.

'Screening Sakamoto: Ryuichi Sakamoto in Two Acts', Crooked Marquee (film-culture magazine), read in full via a text fetch: cast as Captain Yonoi in Nagisa Oshima's Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence (1983) on condition that he also write the score (about three months to compose it), with a soundtrack release just before the Cannes premiere and a vocal version with David Sylvian; on The Last Emperor he was cast as Amakasu with about a week's notice, was asked two days before a reception scene to compose a piece for the on-screen musicians, and after filming was asked by Bertolucci to score half the film to balance the music by David Byrne and Cong Su, with about two weeks to compose and record; he planned a synthesizer score but Bertolucci wanted an orchestral sweep and he delivered it; later acting in Gohatto (1999). Film-writer's essay with Sakamoto's recollections; admiring, with no direct criticism.

Claire Lobenfeld, Sakamoto interview on async, FACT magazine (21 December 2017), read in full via a text fetch: async (2017) has no words or vocals; he said he wanted to focus on the sounds of things; he does field recording wherever he goes, including many recordings in his backyard, and records rain whenever it falls; collaborators on The Revenant (Alva Noto) and the album Glass; the remix compilation async remodels; his favourite current artists named as Vladislav Delay and Demdike Stare; the interviewer ties the album to his career-long interest in nature-attuned sound and to Call Me By Your Name. Interview answered mainly by Sakamoto himself (self-report); his remarks on the 2011 disasters and civilization are political-environmental opinion and were not used.

The Fader, Sakamoto interview on async (5 May 2017), read in full via a text fetch: as a high-school student he catalogued the noises of a crowded train; keeps his ears open to find musical elements in non-musical sound and credits John Cage; treats wrong notes as possible discoveries ('like a gift') while aiming for near-perfection in performance; 'fullmoon' built on a recording of Paul Bowles reading The Sheltering Sky, with Bertolucci's permission and readings in several languages by friends and artist contacts; 'Tri' for three percussionists on triangles, played from a score in one take and repeated more than ten times for machine-like precision; he and Carsten Nicolai performed inside Philip Johnson's Glass House with contact microphones on the glass, which led to the glass pane as an instrument in the live async shows; Shiro Takatani's visuals; time as the album's theme. Interview in his own voice (self-report; never sole support for a row).

Cosmo Lee, review of Alva Noto and Ryuichi Sakamoto, 'insen', PopMatters (2005; 7/10), read in full via a text fetch: Sakamoto performed piano and sent recorded fragments to Carsten Nicolai (credited with additional sound and production), who reshaped them digitally into three-dimensional textures (examples 'Aurora' and 'Iano'); the critic asks, without fully resolving it, why a melody-focused composer would send such material into 'the forest of digital plug-ins', and calls Nicolai's style cold though compelling. Independent critic's review of one collaborative album; mostly favourable with modest reservations (a counter-voice of limited weight).

Jim Green, Yellow Magic Orchestra entry, Trouser Press record guide (trouserpress.com), read in full via a text fetch: lists the group's albums from 1978 to 1985; calls the debut 'merely inane electro-disco' with video-game sounds forced into songs, Solid State Survivor a 'qualitative leap forward', X Multiplies mostly unfunny comedy skits, BGM and Technodelic mixed bags less distinctive than Takahashi's or Sakamoto's solo work, and Service interrupted by comedy tracks; notes Sakamoto was a session keyboardist who met Takahashi while recording his first solo record. Independent critical guide; the main counter-voice on the YMO output.

Wikimedia Commons file page 'RyuichiSakamotoJI4.jpg' (with the Commons API record) -- checked for the portrait: photograph of Ryuichi Sakamoto taken 2 May 2008 by Joi Ito (Joichi Ito), originally posted to Flickr, Commons licence CC BY 2.0 via the Flickr upload bot with the review field naming the photographer (Joi); original 3772 x 2537 pixels. The live Flickr photo page returned a 'no permission to view' (403) response to a signed-out fetch on 2026-10-24, so the Flickr licence could not be re-read live. Rights-basis page; no person-specific claim rests on it.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_rs_rollingstone, src_rs_gac, src_rs_fact, src_rs_fader | 1978-2017 | music-press obituary + institution overview + two interviews] Rolling Stone Australia credits YMO's synthesizer, sequencer and drum-machine pop and says 'Riot in Lagos' (1980) influenced early hip-hop figures; Google Arts & Culture records an early sampler on Technodelic and the 'stateless, exotic' aim; for async he built tracks from field recordings, a looped Paul Bowles reading and a glass pane played with contact microphones. Several independent descriptions of work built on new sound sources, but Trouser Press found the YMO debut 'merely inane electro-disco' and much of the async detail is his own account, so documented at a moderate confidence.

experimentation.rationale: [src_rs_fader, src_rs_fact, src_rs_popmatters, src_rs_gac, src_rs_rollingstone | 1981-2017 | two interviews + critic review + institution overview + obituary] Documented episodes include performing in Philip Johnson's Glass House with contact microphones on the glass and then taking the glass pane into live async shows (Fader), recording rain whenever it falls (FACT), sending piano fragments to Carsten Nicolai to be reprocessed digitally on insen (PopMatters), and the use of a hand-built sampler on Technodelic (Google Arts & Culture). The pattern of trying new sound sources and processes is documented across independent outlets, though the async detail is largely self-reported.

collaboration.rationale: [src_rs_rollingstone, src_rs_crooked, src_rs_oscars, src_rs_popmatters, src_rs_fader | 1978-2017 | obituary + film essay + Academy record + critic review + interview] He co-founded YMO with Takahashi and Hosono, shared the Last Emperor score and Oscar with David Byrne and Cong Su, scored several Bertolucci films, made insen with Carsten Nicolai by exchanging recorded fragments, scored The Revenant with Alva Noto and Bryce Dessner, and invited friends to read for 'fullmoon'. Many documented joint projects with different partners; what the day-to-day working relationships were like is mostly not described.

adaptability.rationale: [src_rs_crooked | 1987 | film-culture essay (the shared-score fact is also in src_rs_oscars and src_rs_rollingstone)] On The Last Emperor he was given about a week's notice to join the shoot, was asked two days before a reception scene for an on-screen piece, then had about two weeks to compose and record half the score; he had planned a synthesizer score but wrote the orchestral sweep Bertolucci wanted. One well-described episode from a single essay, which is otherwise admiring, so a modest score and confidence.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_rs_fader, src_rs_fact, src_rs_popmatters | 1960s-2017 | two interviews + critic review] He says he catalogued the noises of a crowded commuter train as a student, listens for musical elements in non-musical sound, records rain and backyard sound, and calls wrong notes possible 'gifts'; PopMatters describes him as a melody-focused composer. Almost all of the behavioural detail is his own account in two interviews. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 70 / 0.55 lowered to 66 / 0.50 because the support is mainly self-report with only a brief outside characterization.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_rs_rollingstone, src_rs_crooked, src_rs_gac, src_rs_fader | 1978-2017 | obituary + film essay + institution overview + interview] Documented work in synthesizer pop (YMO), film scoring for directors in several countries, acting (Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence, The Last Emperor, Gohatto), solo and collaborative recordings, and live shows with visual artist Shiro Takatani; Rolling Stone Australia reports he had hoped to write a novel or make films. The breadth is documented in several independent sources.

curiosity.rationale: [src_rs_fact, src_rs_fader | 2017 | two interviews] He names current favourites among younger electronic artists (Vladislav Delay, Demdike Stare), credits John Cage as an influence, and describes collecting everyday sounds since school. The signal is real but comes from two interviews in his own voice. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 64 / 0.52 lowered to 62 / 0.48 because it is self-report from one project cycle (async 2017) with no outside description of his habits.

READ (8 cited non-Wikidata sources plus the Commons page): Rolling Stone Australia, Google Arts & Culture, Academy ceremony page, Crooked Marquee, FACT interview, The Fader interview, PopMatters insen review, Trouser Press YMO entry. Blocked or failed: Guardian (page not served / blocked), New York Times (bot wall), Britannica (403), Pitchfork (fetch blocked), Variety (redirected), Grammy artist page (404), Criterion pages (403), Exclaim insen review (page text unavailable). Not opened: books, Japanese-language press, documentary Coda. All text fetches used a summarising reader, so quotations are limited to short phrases. PERSPECTIVES: (1) music-press obituary and film-culture essay, (2) cultural institution and Academy record, (3) independent critics (PopMatters, Trouser Press), (4) Sakamoto's own voice in two interviews (self; never sole support). COUNTER-VOICE: Trouser Press on the weak YMO debut and comedy-skit interruptions and PopMatters' reservation about the processed piano, both modest and about the work not the man. LIMITATIONS: little outside description of working relationships or daily practice, heavy reliance on self-report for async; only film work up to 1987 and async/insen are documented in depth; so no row exceeds 72 or 0.62.
